candidates.title: Even on interim basis, Metra, Union Pacific remain far apart on cost of using rail lines
candidates.excerpt: WASHINGTON — Union Pacific and Metra have dramatically different views of what the commuter operator should pay while the Surface Transportation Board settles their dispute over fees for operating commuter trains on UP tracks in the Chicago area. Metra is essentially seeking to maintain the terms that existed under a purchase of service agreement that expired in June 2025. It says that until a compensation amount is settled, it should continue paying UP according to that contract, which it has been doing. Union Pacific, meanwhile, argues that Metra should pay according to the contract UP imposed on July 1, 2025, as well as back pay beginning in September 2025. Metra also suggests that if additional bond is required, it should reflect the difference between those two contracts, which it estimates at $49.1 million through February 2027, while Union Pacific seeks a bond of $618 million, based on the value of its rail lines. candidates.title: How to repair faulty Industrial Rail couplers
candidates.excerpt: Many years ago, I purchased an O gauge Industrial Rail No. 5003 gondola. It’s a good-looking freight car, but it sometimes uncouples from the rest of its train, usually when rounding a curve but sometimes when it goes over a switch. Do you know if there is a way to repair it? — Stephen Greene Industrial Rail was started by United Model Distributors (UMD) in 1998 and produced a broad range of affordable, traditionally sized O-27 freight cars. The models were made well and featured excellent paint and graphics. Unfortunately, the company lasted only a few years. Production ceased around 2003 or 2004; Atlas purchased the line in 2006. Industrial Rail cars use a variant of Lionel’s magnetic disc coupler design, which first appeared in 1957. candidates.title: Tanker earnings defy all historical comparisons
candidates.excerpt: The tanker market has entered such extraordinary territory that independent owners could be making an additional $400m a day above their original earnings expectations, a windfall that, if sustained for a year, would almost match the entire container shipping industry’s profits during its pandemic-era boom. In its latest weekly report, broker Hartland estimates that independent owners of VLCCs, suezmaxes and aframaxes/LR2s are collectively generating around $400m in daily profits above what they budgeted at the start of 2026. The shipbroker calculates that a month of such earnings represents approximately $12bn in additional profits. A quarter would generate $36bn, while a full year would produce an astonishing $146bn. For context, the world’s containerlines made an estimated $150bn in 2022, their most profitable year on record. candidates.title: US and Europe container spot rates begin to converge
candidates.excerpt: US and Europe container spot rates begin to converge The spreads between spot rates into US and European markets are expected to narrow significantly as US rates go south and rates to Europe head north. Spot rates to the US East Coast are currently more than three times higher than container charges to North Europe from Asia, a spread that Xeneta says is unsustainable. Senior shipping analyst Emily Stausbøll said: “When the spread narrows it will be driven by rates into the US falling and to a much smaller degree Europe strengthening – that is exactly what we are now starting to see.” Xeneta’s latest data shows US rate growth stalling over the last month, at $11,495/feu to the East Coast and $8,296/feu to the West Coast, down 0.1 and 0.2%, respectively. Conversely, European rates have started to climb reaching $2,946/feu a week-on-week increase of 2.5% to North Europe, and $4,165/feu to the Mediterranean, up 3.2%. candidates.excerpt: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action InterManager has called for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety after its latest research highlighted persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. The organisation has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, across tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. Its latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. Over 900 respondents highlighted overly complex paperwork, inadequate time and manpower, commercial pressure, insufficient practical training and a reluctance to address underlying causes. The survey also highlights concerns that inspections can focus on superficial compliance rather than the effectiveness of actual safety practices. candidates.excerpt: Ethanol debut for WinGD as Maersk vessel makes landmark US bunkering and voyage WinGD has recorded the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol fuel engine platform on ethanol fuel, following a successful bunkering and voyage in the US. The 9,000 TEU container ship Tangier Maersk, owned by the Maersk shipping line, successfully sailed from Houston to New York on ethanol fuel. The vessel took on the bunker at the Port of Houston in late September, with the world’s largest bioethanol producer POET supplying fuel for the WinGD X82DF-Mengine powering the vessel. The occasion marked the first marine bunkering of a 100% bioethanol blend in the US, and the first ever in-service bunkering of ethanol to a WinGD engine. As well as highlighting the increasing availability of bioethanol to marine markets – POET alone produces 3 billion gallons a year across 35 sites – the sailing marks a milestone in the operational record of WinGD’s alcohol fuel engine platform. candidates.title: Golden Island delivers world’s largest ethanol bunker stem in Singapore
candidates.excerpt: Golden Island delivers world’s largest ethanol bunker stem in Singapore Golden Island bunkered a Maersk ship with about 5,000 mt of ISCC-certified bio-ethanol in Singapore’s first operation of the kind. Golden Island’s IMO Type II chemical tanker Golden Centaurus supplied the dual-fuel container ship Maersk Halifax while the ship’s containers were being handled. A mass flow meter (MFM) was used in the operation. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said it was the biggest volume of ethanol ever to be delivered in one bunker operation. The stem was nearly twice as large as the 2,800 mt of bio-ethanol that Repsol delivered to the Antonia Maersk in Barcelona in July. The operation was announced last week at a bunker conference in Singapore. The new practice will be led by Rick Bank, managing director and head of private credit and private equity practices at True. The new practice will support appointments including chief executives, chief financial officers, chief operating officers and board members, alongside investment and operational roles within private credit firms. It will also work with TrueBridge, the firm’s interim executive recruitment platform, to provide temporary leadership while permanent appointments are made. “Private credit creates a very different talent question from traditional private equity,” said Bank. “The decision often has to account for where the business is today, what the lender is trying to accomplish and what kind of executive can operate effectively within those conditions. The vessels adopt an innovative integrated charging-and-battery-swapping system using modular box-type power packs, overcoming range limitations for electric vessels via on-site battery hoist swap or direct charging.
